title: Module Header: Osculator = Bézout Coefficient = CF Convergent
content: The module header explains the three-way equivalence at the heart of this proof: the divisibility osculator for d (the integer c with d | 10c−1), the Bézout coefficient gcdA(10,d), and the denominator of the last convergent in the continued fraction expansion of 10/d are all the same object. The imports bring in `Mathlib.Tactic`, `Mathlib.Data.Int.GCD` (for `Nat.gcd_eq_gcd_ab` and `Nat.gcdA`/`Nat.gcdB`), `Mathlib.RingTheory.Coprime.Lemmas` (for `IsCoprime.dvd_of_dvd_mul_left`), and `Proofs.DivisibilityTruncationGeneralOQ01` (for `unified_osculator`, which provides the abstract divisibility equivalence d|n ↔ d|⌊n/10⌋+c·(n%10)). The namespace `DivisibilityTruncationGeneralOQ03` isolates the module, and `open UnifiedOsculator` brings the OQ-01 definitions into scope.
mathContext: The CF/Euclidean duality: Euclid's algorithm for gcd(10,d) proceeds by dividing $r_0 = 10$, $r_1 = d$, $r_2 = r_0 \bmod r_1$, etc. Each quotient $q_k = \lfloor r_{k-1}/r_k \rfloor$ is a CF partial quotient for $10/d$. The final Bézout coefficients $(a, b)$ with $10a + db = 1$ are the numerator/denominator of the last CF convergent. In particular, $a = \text{gcdA}(10,d)$ is the osculator modulo $d$.

title: Bézout Identity Directly Gives the Osculator
content: `bezout_gives_osculator` extracts the osculator from Mathlib's `Nat.gcd_eq_gcd_ab` identity: `gcd(10,d) = 10·gcdA(10,d) + d·gcdB(10,d)`. When `gcd(10,d) = 1` (i.e., d coprime to 10), this gives `1 = 10·gcdA(10,d) + d·gcdB(10,d)`, rearranging to `d | 10·gcdA(10,d) − 1`. The proof uses `linear_combination -hbez` to close the divisibility goal. This is the key observation: the osculator IS the Bézout coefficient, no further construction needed.
mathContext: The modular inverse of 10 mod d is exactly `gcdA(10,d) mod d`. The Bézout identity certifies this directly: if `1 = 10a + db`, then `10a ≡ 1 (mod d)`, so `a` is the inverse and `d | 10a − 1`.

title: Osculator Uniqueness via Coprimality: IsCoprime.dvd_of_dvd_mul_left
content: `osculator_unique_mod` shows any two osculators c, c' satisfy `d | c − c'`. Proof: if `d | 10c − 1` and `d | 10c' − 1`, then `d | 10(c − c')`. Since `gcd(10,d) = 1` (coprimality), `IsCoprime.dvd_of_dvd_mul_left` gives `d | c − c'`. This is the crucial coprimality cancellation: `gcd(10,d) = 1` allows removing the factor 10 from the divisibility.
mathContext: In a UFD (or any integral domain), if `a | bc` and `gcd(a,b) = 1`, then `a | c`. Here: `d | 10(c−c')` and `gcd(d,10) = 1` (note: symmetry of coprimality is used via `.symm`) gives `d | (c−c')`.

title: Part IV: CF Connection — Conceptual Documentation
content: Lines 124–142 are a documentation block explaining why the proof is simpler than originally planned. The CF connection (Euclidean quotients = CF partial quotients, Bézout coefficients = CF convergent numerator/denominator) is informative but not proof-essential for the specific claim in `cf_bezout_correspondence`. That claim asks only: ∃ n ∈ ℕ with n < d and d | 10n−1. This is a pure existence statement that follows from: (1) gcdA(10,d) is an osculator (Bézout), (2) gcdA(10,d) % d ∈ [0,d) (emod), (3) gcdA(10,d) % d is still an osculator (osculator_congr). The CF construction — which would produce the same n as the last convergent denominator — adds only conceptual structure, not proof content.
mathContext: The extended GCD algorithm and CF algorithm for $10/d$ are the same: $q_k = \lfloor r_{k-1}/r_k \rfloor$ appears both as an Euclidean quotient and a CF partial quotient, and the final $(a, b)$ with $10a + db = 1$ equals the last convergent $(p/q)$ with $p = a$ and $q = -b$ (up to sign). The osculator is the denominator $q$, confirming the CF framing. But Lean's `GenContFract` formalism requires significant setup, while the Bézout + emod path is 20 lines.

title: Existential Proof Without Continued Fractions
content: `cf_bezout_correspondence` was originally planned as ~200 lines connecting `GenContFract` and `Nat.xgcd`. The actual proof is ~20 lines: (1) `n₀ := gcdA(10,d) % d` is a non-negative integer in [0,d) (by `Int.emod_nonneg` and `Int.emod_lt_of_pos`); (2) it is still an osculator (by `osculator_mod_d_is_osculator`); (3) `Int.toNat n₀` is the ℕ witness. The `refine ⟨n₀.toNat, ?_, ?_⟩` pattern splits into the bound `n₀.toNat < d` and the osculator property. `omega` closes the bound after casting back via `Int.toNat_of_nonneg`.
mathContext: The existential $\exists n \in \mathbb{N},\ n < d \wedge d \mid 10n - 1$ does not require knowing WHICH convergent of $10/d$ equals $n$. It only needs: a valid osculator exists, and it can be reduced to $[0,d)$. The CF connection is informative but not proof-essential for this particular statement.

title: Canonical Divisibility Rule via Delegation to OQ-01
content: `bezout_osculator_rule` shows `d | n ↔ d | ⌊n/10⌋ + gcdA(10,d)·(n%10)` by directly calling `unified_osculator` from the OQ-01 module. Two arguments are passed: (1) `hcop.isCoprime.symm` converts `Nat.Coprime 10 d` to `IsCoprime d 10` (the argument order required by `unified_osculator`); (2) `bezout_gives_osculator d hcop` provides the osculator witness. The entire divisibility algebra is delegated — OQ-03 contributes only the identification of the canonical osculator.
mathContext: This is a modular architecture: OQ-01 proves the abstract rule $d \mid n \iff d \mid \lfloor n/10 \rfloor + c \cdot (n \bmod 10)$ for any osculator $c$. OQ-03 identifies the canonical $c = \text{gcdA}(10,d)$. Together: the Bézout coefficient IS the divisibility osculator.

title: IsOsculator: Formal Definition and Closure Properties
content: `IsOsculator d c` is defined as the `Prop`: `(d : ℤ) ∣ 10 * c - 1`. Being a bare `Prop` (not a structure) keeps proofs as pure divisibility witnesses. `osculator_shift` shows the osculator set is closed under translation by `d`: the identity `10(c+d) - 1 = (10c-1) + 10d` decomposes into a known divisor plus `d | 10d`. `osculator_congr` generalizes: any `c'` with `d | c' - c` is also an osculator, via `10c' - 1 = (10c-1) + 10(c'-c)`.
mathContext: The set of $d$-osculators is the residue class $\{c_0 + kd : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}$ where $c_0 \equiv 10^{-1} \pmod{d}$. Equivalently, it is a coset of $d\mathbb{Z}$ in $\mathbb{Z}$. `osculator_shift` says this coset is closed under $+d$; `osculator_congr` says it is closed under arbitrary congruence shifts.

title: Canonical Reduction: Three Theorems Pinning the Unique Representative
content: Part III works in three steps. (1) `osculator_mod_d_is_osculator`: applies `osculator_congr` using `d | gcdA(10,d) - gcdA(10,d)%d`, which follows from `Int.ediv_add_emod` rearranged via `linarith`. (2) `osculator_mod_d_bounded`: `Int.emod_nonneg` + `Int.emod_lt_of_pos` give `0 ≤ r < d` as integers; `Int.natAbs_of_nonneg` converts to natural number bound. (3) `canonical_osculator_unique`: chains two applications of `osculator_unique_mod` — `d | c - gcdA` and `d | gcdA - gcdA%d` — then combines with `dvd_add` using the ring identity `c - gcdA%d = (c - gcdA) + (gcdA - gcdA%d)`.
mathContext: The Euclidean (non-negative) remainder satisfies $0 \le r < d$ when $d > 0$. In Lean 4, `Int.emod` implements this: `Int.emod_nonneg : 0 < d → 0 ≤ a % d` and `Int.emod_lt_of_pos : 0 < d → a % d < d`. Converting to `ℕ` uses `Int.toNat_of_nonneg` with the non-negativity proof.

title: Concrete Divisibility Tests: d = 7, 11, 13, 19
content: Five concrete examples instantiate the general theory: `osculator_seven : IsOsculator 7 (−2)` means 7 | 10·(−2) − 1 = −21, checked by `norm_num`. The corresponding divisibility test `div_by_seven`: `7 | n ↔ 7 | (n/10) − 2·(n%10)` applies `unified_osculator` from OQ-01. The d=11 case (c=−1) gives the classical alternating digit sum rule. Each osculator is verified by `norm_num` after unfolding `IsOsculator`.
mathContext: Concrete osculators: 7↔−2 (or +5), 11↔−1 (alternating digit sum), 13↔4, 17↔−5, 19↔2. These are precisely the values of `gcdA(10,d) mod d` for each d, confirming the general theorem.

title: Part VI Summary: d=17 Osculator and Canonical Pipeline
content: `osculator_seventeen` (c=−5, lines 206-207): 7·(−5)−1 = −51 = −3·17, verified by `norm_num`. This completes the five concrete osculators: 7↔−2, 11↔−1, 13↔4, 17↔−5, 19↔2. The final theorem `canonical_divisibility_test` (lines 211-213) is a one-line proof: it simply calls `bezout_osculator_rule d n hcop`, delegating everything to Part I. This demonstrates the layered architecture: Part I proves the full pipeline, and the summary theorem is a zero-cost alias. The three `#check` statements (lines 215-217) serve as self-verification — they confirm the module exports the three key theorems with their expected types, and Lean will flag them as errors if the types were wrong.
mathContext: The d=17 case: $\text{gcdA}(10, 17) = -5$ (since $10 \cdot (-5) + 17 \cdot 3 = -50 + 51 = 1$). The osculator $c = -5$ gives the divisibility test: $17 \mid n \iff 17 \mid \lfloor n/10 \rfloor - 5 \cdot (n \bmod 10)$. For example: $17 \mid 51 \iff 17 \mid 5 - 5 \cdot 1 = 0$ ✓. The positive representative is $17 - 5 = 12$: $17 \mid n \iff 17 \mid \lfloor n/10 \rfloor + 12 \cdot (n \bmod 10)$.
